How to read the numbers

cells.text: Proposal value times chance of winning
Use for a forecast; keep chances honest and revisit after every call
Days logged divided by days sold
At 80 percent with deliverables left, tell the sponsor and agree what moves
Negative means the engagement is losing money; raise it internally first
Compare with the share of days used to see if delivery is on pace

text.text: A proposal is a short argument: here is your problem, here is how we will solve it, here is what it costs.
Structure
The problem in the sponsor's words, with the cost of leaving it.
The approach in three to five phases, each with a deliverable.
Who will do the work, with days per person.
Price, payment terms and what is not included.
Next step and the date the proposal expires.
Before it goes
A second partner has read it
Days sold match the plan, with a buffer
The sponsor has seen the outline before the full document
Decision date and next step are in the proposal row
In the first week
Engagement row created with fee, days sold, start and end dates
Kickoff meeting held with sponsor, team and key stakeholders
Interview list agreed and scheduled
Data request sent with a due date
Weekly check-in booked for the length of the work
The kickoff meeting
Restate the objective and the three questions the work must answer.
Agree how decisions will be made and who can say no.
Confirm how and when the final readout will happen.
Most engagements that go wrong lost their way in the first two weeks.

pages.title: Days sold, days used and margin

text.text: Logging
Log days at the end of each day, in quarters of a day.
Use plain descriptions the partner can scan.
Reading the engagement row

cells.text: Check deliverables sent against days used
Hold a scope conversation with the sponsor

text.text: When days run over
Write down the cause: scope, data, rework or sponsor changes.
Offer the sponsor options: trim, extend, or swap.
Record the decision in the engagement page before more work.
Preparing
Send a pre-read two days before; the meeting is for decisions, not for reading.
Rehearse with the lead once, and walk through the hardest question.
In the room
Start with the answer in one slide.
Show the three findings that matter, each with evidence.
Present options and your recommended path with costs and risks.
End with the decisions you need today and who owns each.
Afterwards
Send the deck and a one-page summary within a day.
Move the engagement to Closed once the last deliverable is accepted.
Ask for a short testimonial and a reference call.
